title: Closer to us than to plants
teaches: Why fungi are a kingdom of their own: chitin walls, digestion outside the body, and DNA that puts them beside animals
summary: **Fungi are not plants.** They have no chlorophyll and make no food; they live on food made by something else.
**Linnaeus filed them with the plants in 1753.** They do not move, which was his test for a plant.
**Whittaker gave them a kingdom of their own in 1969.** Plants make their food, animals swallow it, and fungi digest it outside themselves and absorb it.
**Fungal walls contain chitin.** They are stiffened with the same tough sugar chain as an insect's shell, not the cellulose of plant walls.
**Fungi and animals are each other's closest relatives.** Baldauf and Palmer showed it from several proteins in 1993, and comparisons of whole genomes (every gene an organism has) have confirmed it.
**Some old 'fungi' were not fungi.** Water moulds are kin of brown seaweeds, and slime moulds of amoebas.
**Being close kin has a cost.** Fungal cells work so like ours that drugs which kill fungi tend to harm us, which makes fungal infections hard to treat.

blocks.text: A mushroom comes up out of the ground on a stalk and stays where it is. Bracket fungi grow on trees like shelves. Moulds spread over bread and fruit like a fuzzy lawn. Until well into the twentieth century, fungi were taught in botany classes, stored in herbaria (collections of dried plants) between the mosses and the ferns, and named under the same rules as plants. They are still named under those rules today.[^code]

Yet a fungus does none of the things that make a plant a plant. It has no leaves and no green. It cannot make sugar from light. It does not even take in food the way a plant takes in carbon dioxide and water: it lives on food that something else made, like an animal. The question this lesson follows is what fungi actually are, and the answer, which took until the 1990s to settle, is that they are our relatives more than they are the oak's.

parts.title: The plants that hide their weddings

blocks.text: In 1753 the Swedish botanist Carl Linnaeus published *Species Plantarum*, the book that began the two-part names for plants and fungi still in use, like *Amanita muscaria* and *Quercus robur*. He sorted plants by their flowers, counting stamens and styles. Anything with no visible flowers went into one last class, the **Cryptogamia**, Greek for hidden marriage: ferns, mosses, seaweeds, and fungi. In Linnaeus's scheme there were two kingdoms of living things, animals and plants, and the rule for telling them apart was roughly whether they moved and felt. Fungi did neither, so they were plants.

For more than a century after Linnaeus, the study of fungi was a corner of botany. Its students saw early that fungi were odd. They never had chlorophyll. They lived on dead or living things as food, rather than making their own from sunlight. Their spores were nothing like seeds. But a botanist's tools were a lens and a microscope, and under those tools a fungus looked more like a plant than like anything else: it was built of cells with stiff walls, it stayed put, and it grew by branching, as a root does.

In 1969 the American ecologist Robert Whittaker proposed sorting life into five kingdoms. Bacteria were one, and single-celled creatures with a nucleus another. The three kingdoms of large living things he split by how they get their food. **Plants** make it from light, water and carbon dioxide. **Animals** swallow it and digest it inside a gut. **Fungi** do something else again: they pour digestive enzymes out into their food, let it dissolve outside their bodies, and absorb the small molecules that result through their walls.

That way of eating explains the shape of a fungus. Something that absorbs its food through its surface needs a great deal of surface. A mycelium, a net of tubes a few thousandths of a millimetre wide threading through its food, has far more surface for its bulk than a leaf or an animal's gut. The next lesson looks at how such a tube grows and eats.

blocks.caption: A plant cell, an animal cell and a short piece of a fungal hypha, with the features that set them apart. Not to scale: the hypha is far thinner than either cell is wide.

blocks.text: The chemistry tells the same story. A plant's cell walls are mostly cellulose, long chains of glucose. A fungus's walls are stiffened with **chitin**, chains of a modified glucose with a nitrogen-containing group attached, the same material that hardens a beetle's wing cases and a crab's shell.[^chitin] Plants store spare sugar as starch; fungi store it as glycogen, a branched chain of glucose, as our livers and muscles do. And the fatty molecule that stiffens a fungus's cell membrane, ergosterol, is a close cousin of the cholesterol in ours, whereas plants use a different set of sterols.

Five kingdoms sorted by diet was a better scheme than two sorted by movement, but a diet is a way of life, and unrelated things can share one. The question of who is related to whom could only be settled by comparing the molecules every living thing inherits: its proteins and genes. Two closely related lineages have more similar versions of the same protein, because they have had less time to change apart.

In 1993 Sandra Baldauf and Jeffrey Palmer, at Indiana University, compared four proteins that every cell with a nucleus makes, among them the actin and tubulin that form its internal scaffolding.[^baldauf] Their result, in a paper whose title said so plainly, was that animals and fungi are each other's closest relatives. Plants had branched off earlier. Each protein, analysed separately, gave the same answer, which is what made it convincing.

blocks.caption: Where fungi sit among living things: sorted by looks, as Linnaeus did, and by shared genes and proteins, as since 1993. Only a few branches are shown, and branch lengths mean nothing.
blocks.task: Guess, then compare the two sortings

blocks.text: There was a hint of this all along. The earliest-branching fungi, the chytrids of water and wet soil, make spores that swim with a single tail at the back, as an animal's sperm does. Plants that have swimming cells pull them along with tails at the front. Biologists now group animals and fungi, with a few single-celled relatives, as the **opisthokonts**, Greek for rear tail.[^tail] The two lineages split around a billion years ago, by most estimates. Because plants split off even earlier, a mushroom is a closer cousin of a horse than of the oak it grows under.

The same comparisons threw some old members out. The water moulds, which look and grow very like fungi and include the blight of the Irish potato famine, turned out to be relatives of brown seaweeds and diatoms.[^diatoms] Their walls are mostly cellulose, not chitin. The slime moulds, which crawl as blobs and then put up spore stalks, sit with the amoebas. Each had arrived at a fungus-like way of life on its own: unrelated living things that live the same way often end up looking alike.

parts.title: Why it matters that we are kin

blocks.text: Closeness has one practical consequence. A drug kills a germ by hitting something the germ has and we lack. Bacteria are distant enough that there are many such targets, which is why there are dozens of kinds of antibiotic. Fungal cells, though, run on much the same machinery as ours: the same kinds of ribosomes to build proteins, the same scaffolding, and much the same way of copying DNA. There are few targets a drug can hit in a fungus without hitting us too.

The two main targets that remain are the differences this lesson met. Several antifungal drugs attack ergosterol or stop the fungus making it, and newer ones stop it building its wall. Most of the time, though, fungi are not attacking anyone. This course follows what they do instead: rot the dead, feed living roots, team up with algae as lichens, and fill the soil with threads.

blocks.caption: Five questions on what a fungus is
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: How does a fungus get its food?
choices: It releases enzymes into its food and absorbs what dissolves
It makes sugar from light with a pigment other than chlorophyll
It swallows small pieces of food and digests them inside
items.why: Fungi digest outside their bodies. Enzymes leave the hyphae, break the food down, and the small molecules that result are absorbed through the walls.

items.ask: What stiffening material sets a fungus's cell walls apart from a plant's?
choices: Chitin, as in an insect's shell
Nothing: fungal cells have no walls
items.why: Fungal walls are stiffened with chitin, a chain of a nitrogen-carrying sugar, woven with other polysaccharides. Plants use cellulose, and animal cells have no walls at all.

items.ask: Which evidence best shows that fungi are closer to animals than to plants?
choices: Several proteins and genes compared across many species
Fungi and animals both lack chlorophyll
Fungi and animals both eat food made by others
items.why: Lacking chlorophyll or eating others' food are ways of life that unrelated things can share. Inherited molecules record ancestry, and several proteins, each compared separately, gave the same tree.

items.ask: Why were water moulds long filed with the fungi, though they are not fungi?
choices: They look and live like fungi, threads absorbing food, yet are kin of brown seaweeds
They make mushrooms just like true fungi
They have chitin walls like true fungi
items.why: Water moulds grow as absorbing threads, so they were filed with fungi. Their genes, and their cellulose walls, put them with brown seaweeds and diatoms.

items.ask: Why are infections by fungi harder to treat than infections by bacteria?
choices: Fungal cells work much like ours, so few drugs can kill a fungus without harming us
Fungi are too large for drugs to enter
Fungi have no metabolism for a drug to block
items.why: A drug needs a target the germ has and we lack. Fungi are our relatives, so such targets are few: mainly ergosterol in their membranes and the building of their walls.

code.title: Named as plants
code.text: Fungal names still follow the International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi, and plants, a descendant of the botanists' rules. Animals have a separate code. It is a leftover of history, not a claim about relationships.

chitin.title: Chitin
chitin.text: Chitin is a long chain of N-acetylglucosamine, a glucose with a nitrogen-carrying group attached. It is tough and does not dissolve in water. In fungi it is woven with other sugars into a wall that can hold the pressure of the cell pushing against it.

tail.title: Opisthokonts
tail.text: The name was proposed by Thomas Cavalier-Smith in 1987. Most fungi have lost the swimming cell altogether, but chytrids keep it, which is one reason they are thought to resemble the earliest fungi.

baldauf.title: Four proteins and a plain title
baldauf.text: Baldauf and Palmer's paper in the *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences* was called 'Animals and fungi are each other's closest relatives: congruent evidence from multiple proteins'. That same year, Patricia Wainright and her colleagues reached the same conclusion from ribosomal RNA genes.

diatoms.title: Diatoms
diatoms.text: Diatoms are single-celled algae that build two-part shells of silica, the stuff of glass. Together with brown seaweeds and water moulds they belong to a large group called the stramenopiles.
